Aiges - Driven by curiosity. Built for the extraordinary.

We’re a team of innovators combining AI, software engineering, and data science to redefine astronaut health monitoring. We seek ambitious minds in coding, AI, design, and research who dare to challenge the impossible.

Our vision: Protect life beyond Earth. Push the boundaries of what’s possible.
summary: Aiges lets students, citizen scientists, and astronomers explore how the same patch of sky changes over time. Search by name or coordinates to bring up real NASA SPHEREx infrared observations. Play or blink dated visits, stack or subtract aligned frames, and measure what moves. The shared sky map divides the sky into chunks so people can coordinate where to look. A research assistant can check other astronomy archives for follow-up observations. We tested the workflow on the five challenge targets, including a locked prediction for Epsilon Indi B that landed 0.072 arcseconds from its measured position in an unused visit. Each result links back to evidence that another person can check.
details:
Explore and measure. Aiges queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 observations, downloads FITS cutouts, and aligns them on a common sky grid. Users can select a field of view, compare visits with play, blink, add or subtract, filter by detector, and inspect spectra and quality flags where available. Measurements use the original pixels. The sky map divides the sky into chunks and supports coordinate links. The research assistant can look up follow-up observations in other archives, including NOIRLab's DECam archive.

Evidence. The five challenge targets have 906 saved playback frames. We fit Epsilon Indi B's path using three visits and locked the prediction before inspecting the test visit. Its predicted position was 0.072 arcseconds from the weighted mean position measured in 111 usable test exposures. We also use known objects, stationary controls, and simulated signals to check the pipeline. Four proposed archival linkages were submitted to the Minor Planet Center for review and remain candidates.

Who this helps. A class or astronomy club can open the same images on a laptop, try a measurement, and share the exact sky view and evidence with someone who can check it. Researchers can use a second archive to look for observations that test a promising signal.

Implementation and SI use. The browser app uses React, TypeScript, and Aladin Lite. A FastAPI and Python backend uses Astropy and related scientific libraries for image processing, measurements, and archive queries. Claude Code, ChatGPT, and OpenAI Codex assisted with planning, code, tests, documentation, and submission drafting. The app can use a language model for research assistance when configured. Archive image pixels and measured results come from the published data and astronomy pipeline. A trained spectral classifier scores cold-world spectra.
